svg.aria-label: Diagram: the four documented approaches to granular access control for Amazon S3 data, presented as a ladder driven by policy capacity. AWS states that IAM permission policies and S3 bucket policies are the simplest approach so long as policies fit within the size limits of 20 KB for bucket policies and 5 KB for IAM policies. S3 Access Points offer significantly more policy space because each access point has its own 20 KB policy and thousands exist per Region per account, but require a mechanism for clients to discover the right access point. An IAM session broker scales effectively but requires the customer to build the access-pattern logic. S3 Access Grants expresses permissions as counted grants rather than policy bytes, with one instance per Region per account, 1,000 locations per instance and 100,000 grants per instance, and higher limits available from AWS support. Access Grants also removes the need to map a corporate directory user to an IAM principal, so each CloudTrail data event contains a direct reference to the end user.
svg.title: The ladder is driven by policy size, and each rung costs something different
svg.text: AWS opens the subject with a size limit, not a principle.
Granular access to Amazon S3 data — four approaches, and what moves you along them.
RUNG 1 — IAM policies and bucket policies
“The simplest approach … works, so long as the necessary policies fit within the policy size limits of
S3 bucket policies (20 KB) and IAM policies (5 KB)” — costs nothing, until you run out.
RUNG 2 — S3 Access Points
“thousands of access points per AWS Region per account, with a policy up to 20 KB in size for each”
Cost: “requires a mechanism for clients to discover the right access point for the right dataset”
RUNG 3 — IAM session broker
“supports arbitrarily dynamic permissions patterns and scales effectively”
Cost: “you must build the access-pattern logic”
RUNG 4 — S3 Access Grants: stop measuring bytes, start counting rows
1 instance per Region per account · 1,000 locations per instance · 100,000 grants per instance
“a simplified model … by prefix, bucket, or object”, granting read-only, write-only or read-write.
“contact AWS support to request higher limits” — a quota can be asked for; a 20 KB document size cannot.
And the part that is not about capacity at all
With IAM Identity Center trusted identity propagation, applications “no longer need to first map the
user to an IAM principal” — so each CloudTrail data event carries “a direct reference to the end user”.
“You no longer need to reconstruct the relationship between different users and IAM sessions.”
Cost is organisational: it “requires collaboration between” the service and Identity Center administrators.
The audit: measure your largest bucket policy against 20 KB.
That one number says which rung you are on, and whether this topic is urgent or theoretical. Most estates are
nowhere near. A few are at 19 KB and do not know it.
Then settle who owns the Access Grants instance: locations are plural, grants are plural, the instance is not —
so the first team to need one creates it for everybody in that account and Region.
